QUESTION ADDRESSED  IN THIS BRIEF
Whether Arizona’s state -designed voter registration form, which requires documentary proof of citizenship, is “equivalent” to a federal voter registration
form that does not require such documentary proof, as
required by Section 7 of the National Voter Registration Act of 1993.

INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE 1
Dēmos is a nonprofit, nonpartisan public policy organization dedicated to building a more inclusive democracy and economy. For over  twenty-five years,
Dēmos has worked at the intersection of democracy reform, economic justice, and racial justice, drawing on
research, policy development, legal advocacy, grassroots partnerships, and coalition-building.
Dēmos has long supported the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (“NVRA”) and has conducted extensive research, advocacy, and monitoring regarding
NVRA compliance. As part of that work, Dēmos has
researched the impact of Section  7 of the NVRA on
voter registration. See, e.g. , Food Rsch. & Action Ctr.
& Dēmos, How an Important Federal Law Can Help
Millions of Low -Income People Register to Vote
Through State Public Assistance Agencies  (2019);
Laura Williamson, Pamela Cataldo & Brenda Wright,
Dēmos, Toward a More Representative Electorate: The
Progress and Potential of Voter Registration through
Public Assistance Agencies (2018); J. Mijin Cha,
Dēmos, Registering Millions: The Success and Potential of the National Voter Registration Act at 20 (2013);
Lisa J. Danetz & Scott Novakowski, Dēmos, Expanding Voter Registration for Low -Income Citizens: How

2

North Carolina is Realizing the Promise of the National Voter Registration Act (2008).
Dēmos has also served as counsel in actions to enforce state and local compliance with Section 7 in several covered states. See, e.g., Valdez v. Squier, 676 F.3d
935 (10th Cir. 2012) (New Mexico);  Harkless v. Brunner, 545 F.3d 445 (6th Cir. 2008) (Ohio); Action NC v.
Strach, 216 F. Supp. 3d 597 (M.D.N.C. 2016) (North
Carolina); Delgado v. Galvin , 2014 WL 1004108 (D.
Mass. Mar. 14, 2014) (Massachusetts); Ass’n of Cmty.
Orgs. for Reform Now v. Scott, 2008 WL 2787931 (W.D.
Mo. July 15, 2008) (Missouri).  Dēmos’s longstanding
work in NVRA compliance demonstrates its  expertise
in the field and underscores the critical role that the
NVRA, and specifically Section 7, has played in expanding voting access across the country, particularly
in communities of color and among low-income voters.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Section 7 of the NVRA requires state offices offering public assistance to distribute mail voter registration forms “with each application for … assistance.” 52
U.S.C. § 20506(a)(6)(A). The office may distribute the
“form described in [Section 9(a)(2)]” of the NVRA (the
“federal form”), id., which is designed by the Election
Assistance Commission using the criteria set forth in
NVRA Section 9(b). Or the office may distribute “the
office’s own form if it is equivalent to the form described in [Section 9(a)(2)].” Id. The record in this case
suggests, and the parties appear to assume, that

3


public assistance offices in Arizona provide only a
state-designed voter registration form.
Arizona’s state form requires documentary proof of
citizenship (“DPOC”). The federal form does not . This
brief addresses whether Arizona’s state form is “equivalent” to the federal one within the meaning of Section 7.
Two things are equivalent when they are equal in
the relevant way. This standard does not require perfect identity but rather equality according to a specific
metric. Petitioner proposes that the proper standard is
similarity, not equality, but dictionaries in print at the
NVRA’s passage, infra § I.A, and Congress’s practice
when enacting other statutes, infra § I.B, refute that
contention. The NVRA’s structure and preamble round
out the analysis. They prove that the relevant measure
of equivalence is administrative burden on the applicant, so that substituting a state form for the federal
form does not become a vehicle for introducing additional obstacles to voter registration. Infra § I.C.
Petitioner’s contrary view, supported by other
aligned parties, is that a state form is equivalent to the
federal form as long as it meets the  criteria for mail
voter registration forms set out in Section  9(b). But
Congress used different language in different provisions to address different requirements: the NVRA requires compliance with Section 9(b) —a requirement
codified in Section 6 of the statute—and it additionally
requires equivalence to the federal form when states

4

provide their form as a replacement  for that federal
form—a require ment codified in Section 7 . Infra
§ I.D.1. Petitioner’s reading is also irreconcilable with
the NVRA’s drafting history. Infra § I.D.2.
Applying the proper meaning of Section  7, it is
clear that Arizona’s form does not satisfy the equivalence standard. People who use public assistance offices generally have lower incomes and educational attainment than the national average. For that population especially, seemingly routine administrative burdens can substantially affect voter registration rate s.
Infra § II.A. The burden of providing DPOC is often
substantial, as  the district court’s findings of fact in
this case—rendered after a trial on the merits —confirm. Infra § II.B. Because Arizona’s form and the federal form do not impose equal administrative burdens,
the Ninth Circuit correctly concluded that Arizona’s
form is not “equivalent” under Section 7.
ARGUMENT
I. The NVRA’s equivalence standard requires a substitute state form to impose no
greater burden on registering to vote than
the federal form.
Section 7 of the NVRA requires any state -created
voter registration form distributed by a state public assistance office in lieu of the federal voter registration
form to be “equivalent” to the federal form. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20506(a)(6)(A)(ii). The NVRA’s text, purpose, and
structure establish that two forms are “equivalent” for

5


purposes of Section 7 when they impose equal administrative burdens on people registering to vote. Petitioner’s reading of Section  7, under which two forms
are equivalent as long as they “meet[] [Section  9(b)’s]
criteria for the contents of a voter- registration form,”
Br. for Pet’r 29, is irreconcilable with the NVRA’s
structure and refuted by its drafting history.
A. The plain meaning of “equivalent”
denotes things that are equal in
some relevant respect.
The ordinary meaning of “equivalent,” in 1993 and
today, is “relevantly equal.” Equivalence presupposes
a specific measure of comparison; two things are equivalent when they are the same in ways that matter. To
borrow an example from this Court’s own usage, two
statutory provisions are “equivalents” when they “resembl[e]” one another in “all relevant respects.” BNSF
Ry. Co. v. Loos, 586 U.S. 310, 317–18 (2019).
Dictionaries contemporaneous with the NVRA’s
passage support this interpretation. Across a wide
range of dictionaries in print in 1993, “equivalent” is
defined with reference to equality across some specific
measure:
• “1.a. Equal, as in value, force, or meaning.
b. Having similar or identical effects.” Equivalent, American Heritage Dictionary (3d ed.
1992).

6

• “A. [] Equal in value, power, efficacy, or import.”
Equivalent, Oxford English Dictionary (2d ed.
1989).
• “1. equal in quantity, value, force, meaning,
etc.” Equivalent, Webster’s New World Dictionary (3d coll. ed. 1988).
• “1. equal in force, amount, or value.” Equivalent,
Webster’s Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary
(1988).
• “1. equal in value, measure, force, effect, significance, etc.” Equivalent , Random House Dictionary of the English Language (2d ed. 1987).
• “Of equal value, weight, force, etc.” Equivalent ,
Ballentine’s Law Dictionary (3d ed. 1969).
And, as Petitioner and the United States  emphasize, Black’s Law Dictionary defined “equivalent” as
“[e]qual in value, force, measure, volume, power, and
effect or having equal or corresponding import, meaning or significance; alike, identical.” Equivalent ,
Black’s Law Dictionary (6th ed. 1990); see Br. for
Pet’r 28; Br. for United States 22 . While such definitions do not require equivalent things to be the same
in all respects, they each require equality along the dimension relevant to the comparison.
Petitioner notes that two dictionaries say “equivalent” can mean “alike” or “having similar … effects.”
See Br. for Pet’r 28; see also Br. for U.S. as Resp’t in

7


Supp. of Pet. in No. 25 -1017 and in Opp. to Pets. in
Nos. 25-1019 and 25-1022, at 20–21 (“Similar in function or effect[,] rather than identical.”) (quoting Pet.
App. 179a). From there, Petitioner concludes that Section 7 requires forms to be only “similar” in the relevant way. Br. for Pet’r 28. That cherry-picked interpretation of “equivalent” cannot be reconciled with the
statute in which the term is found, as set out in § I.D,
infra. But even as a pure textual matter, that argument fails: the OED , Webster’s New World, Random
House, and Ballentine’s say nothing about similarity ,
even in secondary definitions . The far more common
meaning—present in every dictionary and absent in
none—focuses on equality . Equality is not similarity.
Compare Equal, American Heritage Dictionary (3d ed.
1992) (“1. Having the same quantity, measure, or
value as another. … 7. Showing or having no variance
in proportion, structure, or appearance.”), with Similar, id. (“1. Related in appearance or nature; alike
though not identical.”).
B. In other statutes, Congress uses
“equivalent” to mean “relevantly
equal.”
Amicus’s understanding of how Congress used the
term “equivalent” in the NVRA matches how the term
is used in other statutes. Congress ordinarily uses
“equivalent” to require equality (not mere similarity)
with respect to a benchmark that aligns with the statute’s purpose. Although the things being compared

8

need not be identical in every respect, they must be
equal in the way that the statute identifies:
1. The Americans with Disabilities Act  of 1990 requires transportation providers to furnish disabled individuals with a level of service “equivalent to the level
of service provided to the general public.” 42 U.S.C.
§ 12184(b)(3)–(5).
2. The Internal Revenue Code uses “equivalent” to
describe legal relationships that receive the same
treatment as a specified baseline. It refers to service
“recognized as equivalent to employment,” 26 U.S.C.
§ 3121(b); a foreign government that grants an “equivalent exemption,” id.  § 3121(b)(12)(B); and payments
“equivalent to the sum of the taxes” that otherwise
would be due, id.  § 3121(l)(1)(A). In each instance,
Congress identified a point of comparison and asked
whether the substitute was equal with respect to that
benchmark.
3. ERISA permits retirement plans to offer lump
sum payments in addition to annuities, so long as the
lump sum is the “actuarial equivalent” of the annuity.
29 U.S.C. §  1054(c)(3). “Equivalence,” in this context,
means that the value of the two options must be the
same from an actuary’s point of view. Thus, “[r]eceiving $1000 45 days from now is not equivalent to receiving $1000 now, because (among other things) that
$1000 can earn interest every day one has it.” Stephens
v. U.S. Airways Grp. , 644 F.3d 437, 442 (D.C. Cir.
2011) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in the judgment).

9


When Congress wishes to permit similarity instead
of equality, it uses different language —usually, by
specifying “substantial equivalence,” as it did in its
first draft of the NVRA, see infra § I.D.2:
a. The Dodd -Frank Act , for example, allows the
Federal Insurance Office to preempt state law for a foreign insurer that agrees to provide consumer protections “substantially equivalent to the level of protection achieved” by state regulations , 31 U.S.C.
§ 313(f)(2)(B)—and defines that term to mean
“achiev[ing] a similar outcome,” id. § 313(r)(9). See Antonin Scalia & Bryan A. Garner, Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts 228 (2012) (“[T]he meaning
of [a] definition is almost always closely related to the
ordinary meaning of the word being defined.”).
b. Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic
Act, a medical device can be deemed “substantially
equivalent” to a “legally marketed device” despite having “different technological characteristics” if it has
“the same intended use” and “is as safe and effective”
as the predicate. 21 U.S.C. § 360c(i)(1)(A).
c. The Job Training Partnership Act funded jobtraining programs so long as no trainee would be hired
for a job “when any other individual is on layoff from
the same or any substantially equivalent job.” 29
U.S.C. §  1553(b)(3) (1994) (repealed 1998) ; Congress
could not have been clearer that it meant “same or similar.”

10

d. And the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act requires foreign issuers of securities to make
certain disclosures in any form that “is the equivalent
of, or substantially similar to,” the SEC’s Form 10 -K
or Form 20 -F, 15 U.S.C. §  7214a(a)(3)(B)(i), again
showing that equivalence and substantial similarity
are different concepts.
Petitioner elides the difference between “equivalence” and “substantial equivalence,” but they are not
synonyms. The modifier “substantially” usually permits some degree of deviation from the relevant benchmark. See Substantially, Black’s Law Dictionary (6th
ed. 1990) (“Essentially; without material qualification;
in the main; in substance; materially; in a substantial
manner”); Substantial, Webster’s Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary (1988) (“being largely but not wholly
that which is specified”);  Victor v. Nebraska, 511
U.S. 1, 19 (1994) (quoting one definition for “substantial” from Webster’s Third New International Dictionary (1981) as “that specified to a large degree”).
“Equivalent,” when used alone and unmodified, demands closer correspondence. See supra § I.A.
C. For purposes of the NVRA, the relevant measure of equivalence is the
burden a form imposes on voter registration.
The “relevant respect” in which a state’s form must
be equivalent to the federal form under Section 7 of the
NVRA is with respect to the burdens the form imposes
on voter registration. The measure of equivalence is

11


whether differences between the forms impair the opportunity to register to vote that the federal form provides. That is clear both from the NVRA’s statutory
purpose and from its structure.
First, Section 2 of the NVRA explains that Congress regarded voting as a “fundamental right” that
state and federal governments have a “duty … to promote.” 52 U.S.C. § 20501(a). Congress’s purposes were
explicit and four-fold: to “increase the number of eligible citizens who register to vote,” id. § 20501(b)(1); enable implementation “in a manner that enhances the
participation of eligible citizens as voters,” id.
§ 20501(b)(2); “protect the integrity of the electoral
process,” id. § 20501(b)(3); and “ensure that accurate
and current voter registration rolls are maintained,”
id. § 20501(b)(4). See also Project Vote/Voting for Am.
v. Long, 682 F.3d 331, 334 (4th Cir. 2012) (Wilkinson,
J.). A form that requires more documentation than the
federal form necessarily is not equally capable of satisfying the NVRA’s statutory purpose of “increas[ing]
the number of eligible citizens who register to vote” or
“enhanc[ing] the participation of eligible citizens as
voters.” 52 U.S.C. § 20501(b).
Where, as here, Congress writes a preamble for  a
statute setting forth its intentions , that preamble informs the statute’s meaning. See  Bittner v. United
States, 598 U.S. 85, 98– 99 (2023)  (considering the
Bank Secrecy Act’s enacted “statement of purpose” as
“evidence” of statutory meaning); see also County of
Maui v. Haw. Wildlife Fund, 590 U.S. 165, 174 (2020)

12

(considering the Clean Water Act’s enacted declaration of policy to determine the statute’s meaning );
Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637, 649 (2013)
(relying on legislative findings that “highlight[ed] the
primary problem that the statute was intended to
solve”).2 Indeed, this Court has relied on the NVRA’s
preamble in the past to inform its understanding of
specific statutory provisions. See Arizona v.  Inter
Tribal Council  of Ariz., Inc. , 570 U.S. 1, 13 (2013)
(quoting 42 U.S.C. §  1973gg(b), now codified at 52
U.S.C. § 20501(b)).
Second, the NVRA’s structure confirms that the
relevant measure of equivalence is administrative burden on the act of voter registration. As this Court held
in Inter Tribal Council , the NVRA’s standards for
voter registration forms are safeguards against state -
created administrative burdens. 570 U.S. at 11– 12.
Section 6(a), which governs mail voter registration, requires states to “accept and use” the federal form even
when they exercise the option to create a parallel state
form. 52 U.S.C. § 20505(a). The availability of the federal form, which must be accepted alongside any state
form, serves as insurance for Congress’s statutory

2 See also Scalia & Garner  at 218 (“[A] prologue can[] be considered in determining which of various permissible meanings the
dispositive text bears.”); Samuel L. Bray, The Mischief Rule, 109
Geo. L.J. 967, 994 & n.146 (2021) (a statute’s “mischief” can be
determined “by examination of the statute itself, especially if
there are enacted findings.”); id. at 1002–03 (defending the mischief rule on textualist grounds  as a guide to “context and pragmatic enrichment”).

13


purpose of facilitating voter registration. Congress ensured that states would  accept the federal form to
“guarantee[] that a simple means of registering to vote
in federal elections [would] be available” “[n]o matter
what procedural hurdles a State’s own form imposes.”
Inter Tribal Council, 570 U.S. at 12.
Section 7 also serves this function, set ting out additional and separate conditions for a state to provide
its own form in lieu of the federal form . In Section 7 ,
the NVRA uses an all -important disjunctive —or—to
show that “the office’s own form” may displace the federal form entirely. See 52 U.S.C. § 20506(a)(6)(A).
The equivalence requirement of Section 7 replaces
the insurance provided by an applicant’s access to the
federal form. By requiring equivalence, Congress guaranteed that a state’s substitute form could not present
greater obstacles to voter registration  at a public assistance office than the federal form does. Petitioner’s
reading allows states to use Section 7(a)(6)(A)(ii)’s substitution to end-run the NVRA’s “backstop” and make
their “procedural hurdles” mandatory. See Inter Tribal
Council, 570 U.S. at 12.
Acknowledging that Section 7’s equivalence requirement creates independent obligations  when
states choose to supplant the federal form with their
own does not interpret the NVRA to “take with one
hand what [it] provides in the other.” Contra  Br. for
United States 23. The NVRA is not a grant of authority to the states . It is a safeguard of  voting rights, a

14

vindication of federal interests in promoting election
participation, and an exercise of Congress’s constitutional power to displace state election law . See Inter
Tribal Council, 570 U.S. at 13–14. In pursuit of those
goals, the statute imposes  an “equivalence” standard
when a state decides to make its own form available as
the sole or default means of registering to vote in federal elections, to address a specific risk to voters that
arises when a state makes that choice.
Nor is this reading overly formalistic. Not every difference between forms creates an “equivalence” problem; a state need not reproduce the federal form word
for word. It might, for example, request the registrant’s county of residence, or collect less demographic
information than the federal form does. Indeed, Arizona’s own form contains several features absent from
the federal form, including a QR code, optional demographic questions, and early -voting enrollment options. See Ariz. Sec’y of State, Arizona Voter Registration Form (rev. Dec. 2025), https://azsos.gov/sites/default/files/docs/AZ-State-Voter-Registration-Form-Dec
2025-fillable.pdf [ https://perma.cc/6WLG-F7HL].
These changes would not violate Section  7’s equivalence requirement as long as they did not increase the
administrative burden on the registrant or create a n
obstacle to voter registration. But a requirement that
could cause an otherwise registrable applicant to be
rejected, or that requires an applicant to undertake
greater burdens to furnish something that the federal
form does not require, is qualitatively different from

15


an inconsequential variation in, for example, formatting or information collection.3
D. Petitioner’s reading of “equivalent”
is inconsistent with the statute.
Neither Petitioner nor the parties aligned with it
consider the NVRA’s preamble  or these aspects of its
broader structure, and that oversight leads their niche
constructions of “equivalent” badly astray. Petitioner
is correct that “[t]wo forms can be ‘equivalent’ in different respects,” and that the key question for this
Court is “in what way” Section 7 requires forms to be
equivalent. Br. for Pet’r 28– 29. But Petitioner errs by
concluding equivalence requires only similarity of effect or function, or some form of substantial equivalence, making Arizona’s form “equivalent” to the federal form under the NVRA because Arizona “accepts
it” for the purpose of registering voters. Br. for
Pet’r 29. Petitioner’s reading drains the term “equivalent” of any meaning: Any form is equivalent in that
way so long as the state says the purpose and effect of
the form are voter registration, no matter what the

3 The difference the Ninth Circuit identified between Arizona’s
state form and the federal form did not result , as Petitioner insists, in a ban on all variations. Contra Br. for Pet’r 30. As the
Ninth Circuit explained, it found the two forms non- equivalent
because one form would reject applicants that the other would
accept. See Pet. App. 51a–52a (“If applicants who do not include
DPOC use the state form, they will not be registered as federal -
only voters but if they use the federal form, they will be registered.”).

16

form says or what varying effects on registration it
may have compared to the federal form.
To avoid that strange result, Petitioner and its allied parties attempt to anchor their understanding of
Section 7’s equivalence requirement in Section  9(b)’s
separate requirements for the contents of federal and
state voter registration forms. 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1).
See Br. for Pet’r 29; Br. for Resp’ts Petersen & Montenegro 15; Br. for United States 22–24. That move does
not make sense for at least two reasons.
1. Section 7’s equivalence requirement is distinct from Section 9(b)’s
content requirements for voter
registration forms.
The term “equivalent” in Section 7 requires a comparison with the federal form that is different from the
inquiry into whether a state form meets Section 9(b)’s
threshold requirements for any state or federal mail
voter registration form. Section 9(b), for  example, requires that a voter registration form may “only” require information that is “necessary” to assess eligibility or administer elections. 52 U.S.C. §  20508(b)(1).
Section 7 addresses a more specific situation where  a
state opts to substitute its “own form” for the federal
form in public assistance offices; it may do so only if its
form both meets the criteria of Section 9(b) and is
“equivalent to the form described in [Section 9(a)(2)].”
Id. § 20506(a)(6)(A)(ii).

17


Section 7 does not refer to Section 9(b) at all; it does
not need to, because the requirement to meet the Section 9(b) criteria is already set by Section 6 of the
NVRA. Section 6 allows a state to develop and use its
own mail voter registration form alongside the federal
form only if it “ meets all of the criteria stated in [Section 9(b)].” 52 U.S.C. § 20505(a)(2) (emphasis added).
Petitioner’s reading collapses two different statutory provisions into one another, rendering Section 7’s
equivalence requirement redundant . But Congress
used different language in Sections 6 and 7 to prescribe distinct obligations, and this difference in language must be given effect. If Congress wanted to permit states’ “own form[s]” to fully displace the federal
form based solely on satisfaction of Section 9(b)’s criteria, Congress could have used the same language in
Section 7 that it used in Section 6. But it did not. Rather, Section 7  requires a direct comparison between
the state’s form and the federal form. Where Congress
uses different language in two provisions of the same
statute, this Court ascribes different meaning to those
provisions. See, e.g., M & K Emp. Sols., LLC v. Trs. of
IAM Nat’l Pension Fund , 608 U.S. 264, 274 (2026);
Gallardo ex rel. Vassallo v. Marstiller, 596 U.S. 420,
429–30 (2022); Russello v. United States, 464 U.S. 16,
23 (1983) (“[Where] Congress includes particular language in one section of a statute but omits it in another
section of the same Act, it is generally presumed that
Congress acts intentionally.”); see also Scalia & Garner
at 170 (“[W]here the document has used one term in
one place, and a materially different term in another,

18

the presumption is that the different term denotes a
different idea.”). Yet Petitioner’s reading does the opposite.
Arizona’s DPOC requirement may violate both provisions. But even if this Court concludes that the requirement satisfies Section 9(b), it must separately determine whether a state form imposing that requirement is equivalent to the federal form under Section 7.
The better reading of Section 7 gives effect to Congress’s deliberate choice to require the use of the federal form or its “equivalent” to ensure accessible registration for some of the nation’s most vulnerable voters.
2. Petitioner’s reading is inconsistent
with Section 7’s drafting history.
Petitioner and its allied parties seek to read “equivalent” to mean roughly or substantially equivalent, affording Arizona flexibility to impose requirements that
make registering to vote more burdensome than it
would be using the federal form. Br. for Pet’r  28. Section 7’s drafting history  confirms they are wrong. See
Caleb Nelson, Statutory Interpretation  364 (1st ed.
2011) (noting that some find drafting history to be a
“more powerful form of legislative history … than floor
debates and even committee reports.”).
Congress considered and rejected a version of Section 7 that would have required mere “substantial
equivalence,” a standard that resembles Petitioner’s
preferred similarity requirement. As introduced on the
House floor, H.R. 2 (which became the NVRA) required

19


a public assistance office’s form to be “substantially
equivalent” to the federal form. H.R.  2, 103d Cong.
§ 7(a)(6)(A)(ii) (as introduced Jan. 5, 1993). Soon after,
in a markup session, Representative Al Swift, who introduced the bill on the House floor, see 139 Cong. Rec.
253 (Jan. 5, 1993), moved to strike the word “substantially.” The committee adopted that amendment by
voice vote, see H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at 2 (1993), as reprinted in 1993 U.S.C.C.A.N. 105, 106; H.R.  2, 103d
Cong. § 7(a)(6)(A)(ii) (as reported by H. Comm. on H.
Admin., Feb. 2, 1993), and the change was adopted by
the full House and Senate without further comment. 4
See H.R. 2, 103d Cong. §  7(a)(6)(A)(ii) (as received by
Senate, Feb. 17, 1993).
Petitioner’s reading would make this amendment
pointless. “It is axiomatic that a statute should not be
read to implicitly include language specifically rejected.” Dai Glob., LLC v. Adm’r of the U.S. Agency for
Int’l Dev. , 945 F.3d 1196, 1199 (Fed. Cir. 2019); see
Acosta v. Loc. Union 26, UNITE HERE, 895 F.3d 141,
144 (1st Cir. 2018) (Souter, J., ret.) (“Few principles of
statutory construction are more compelling than the
proposition that Congress does not intend sub silentio
to enact statutory language that it has earlier

a bill that included “substantially equivalent.” See S. 2, 103d
Cong. §  7(a)(6)(A)(ii) (as introduced in Senate , Jan. 21, 1993).
Senator Ford abandoned that bill in favor of one incorporating the
House’s amendment. See S. 460, 103d Cong. § 7(a)(6)(A)(ii) (as reported Feb. 25, 1993). In other words, the Senate, like the House,
was made aware of the difference that Petitioner seeks to elide.

20

discarded in favor of other language.”) (quoting INS v.
Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 442– 43 (1987) ).
“Where Congress includes limiting language in an earlier version of a bill but deletes it prior to enactment,
it may be presumed that the limitation was not intended.” Russello, 464 U.S. at 23–24.
Congress considered and rejected not only Petitioner’s preferred statutory standard but also its preferred specific result . During debates on the Senate
floor, Senator Simpson introduced an amendment
providing that “[n]othing in [the NVRA would] be construed to preclude a state from requiring presentation
of documentary evidence of the citizenship of an applicant for voter registration.” 139 Cong. Rec. 5098 (Mar.
16, 1993). The Senate adopted the amendment. Id. at
5099; see H.R. 2, 103d Cong. §  13 (as passed by the
Senate, Mar. 17, 1993).
Because H.R. 2 , as passed by the Senate , differed
from the version passed by the House, the bill went to
a conference committee, which rejected the change.
See Br. for Resp’ts Mi Familia Vota & Voto Latino 29
(discussing Congress’s rejection of the amendment);
Br. for AZ AANHPI Resp’ts 22–23 (same). An attempt
to restore the measure failed on the House floor, see
139 Cong. Rec. 9228, 9231 (May 5, 1993), and the conference version became law.
The failure of the Simpson Amendment reflects
Congress’s collective decision -making while enacting
the NVRA. This is “enactment history, not the fog of

21


words generated by legislators,” and it is  especially
probative of statutory meaning. See S. Austin Coal.
Cmty. Council v. SBC Commc’ns Inc. , 274 F.3d 1168,
1172 (7th Cir. 2001) (Easterbrook, J.) (drawing a similar inference from a n accepted amendment that
broadened the scope of the relevant statute); County of
Maui, 590 U.S. at 176 (Congress’s “reject[ion of] … [an]
amendment that would have extended the [Clean Water Act’s] permitting provision to groundwater”
“strongly support[ed]” an inference that the permitting
provision did not reach groundwater).
The Simpson Amendment’s history “consists of actions taken by legislative bodies, not just words
penned by staffers or lobbyists.” Gonzalez v. Arizona ,
677 F.3d 383, 441 (9th Cir. 2012) (en banc) (Kozinski,
C.J., concurring), aff’d sub nom. Arizona v. Inter Tribal
Council of Ariz., Inc., 5 70 U.S. 1 (2013). This Court
“has recognized that such drafting history can offer interpretive insight,” id. at 441 ( discussing Hamdan v.
Rumsfeld, 548 U.S. 557 (2006)), and it is probative (to
the extent the Court finds “the statutory language is
in equipoise”) that “both chambers affirmatively rejected efforts to authorize precisely what Arizona is
seeking to do,” id. at 442.
*
Statutory text, structure, and history all point in
the same direction. Congress did not use “equivalent”
to mean “similar.” It did not make compliance with
Section 9(b) the sole measure of equivalence under

22

Section 7. And it did not authorize states to replace the
federal form with a substitute that imposes additional
burdensome registration requirements such as DPOC.
II. Arizona’s voter registration form and the
federal form are not “equivalent” within
the meaning of Section 7.
Arizona’s voter registration form requires documentary proof of citizenship, and the federal form does
not. Compare Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-121.01(C), and Pet.
App. 194a –95a, with U.S. Elec. Assistance Comm’n,
OMB Control No. 3265-0015, Register to Vote in Your
State by Using this Postcard Form and Guide 2 (setting forth application instructions for the federal
form), https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/eac_assets/1/6/Federal_Voter_Registration_ENG.pdf
[https://perma.cc/LZ88-7B5A]. Amicus’s experience
shows, and the district court’s findings confirm, that
this difference imposes an administrative burden that
is not equivalent to the burdens created by the federal
form, and which is particularly felt by the population
Section 7 targets.
A. Even seemingly minor administrative burdens substantially affect
voter registration, especially for the
applicants Section 7 was designed to
reach.
Amicus’s experience shows that even routine administrative burdens in the registration process can
substantially affect registration  rates. For example,

23


after Massachusetts settled with amicus’s clients in
Delgado v. Galvin , No.  12-cv-10872 (D. Mass.), the
state mailed voter -registration applications with prepaid return envelopes to users of public  assistance offices to address the obstacle of finding a stamp and an
envelope. See Rachana Bhatt, Evgenia Dechter &
Richard Holden, Registration Costs and Voter Turnout, 176 J. Econ. Behav. & Org. 91, 93 & n.6 (2020).
That minor intervention produced a statistically significant increase in voter registration. Id. at 98.
This example reflects the reality that the citizens
Section 7 was designed to reach are more severely affected by administrative burdens than the average
American. Section 7 provides registration opportunities to voters who are “less likely to own cars and,
therefore, less likely to interact with a motor vehicle
office.” Scott Novakowski & Youjin B. Kim, Dēmos, Increasing Access in Hard Times: Women and the National Voter Registration Act 3 (2010). Voters who register at public assistance agencies have disproportionately low income and levels of educational

attainment.5 Administrative burdens are particularly
consequential for such voters.6

CONCLUSION
Because Arizona’s state form is more burdensome
to complete than the federal form, the Ninth Circuit
correctly concluded that it is not “equivalent” to the
federal form under Section 7(a)(6)(A)(ii) of the NVRA.
